BeHistorical · Canvas paste kit

Canvas Calendar Events

How to paste one of these

One event per topic, shared by both rooms. The dates live in Canvas’s Assign to, one row per section, using the table printed with each event.

  1. Canvas Calendar, click the day, Edit, then More Options.
  2. Title the event exactly as given (use Copy title).
  3. In the Rich Content Editor click the </> icon to open the HTML editor. Never paste into the visual editor: it collapses the table.
  4. Press Copy HTML and paste the whole block.
  5. Switch back to the visual editor, delete [INSERT ASSIGNMENT LINK], and insert the real assignment from the course-links panel on the right. Do not hand-type that link.
  6. In Assign to, add one row per section from the table, remove the Everyone row, and save.

AP World History · Foundations
Topic F0: Intro to BeHistorical
GGreen DayThursday, August 6 SSilver DayFriday, August 7

OVERVIEW

Day 0 is the frame for the whole year. Before you learn a single date, you need to know what this course is asking you to become: a historian, with six specific habits of mind. Today you meet the six AP historical thinking skills in plain language, walk through the 10-module rhythm you will see in every class, and write a baseline snapshot of yourself as a historian on Day 1. That baseline becomes the first entry in the Historian's Portfolio you receive in May.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can name the six AP historical thinking skills and give a one-sentence explanation of each in my own words.
  • I can describe the 10-module structure I will see in every BeHistorical lesson and explain what each module trains.
  • I can explain what my Historian's Portfolio is and write a baseline self-portrait as a historian, where I am today and where I want to be by May.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can list the six skills (contextualization, comparison, causation, continuity/change, argumentation, sourcing) and give a plain-language definition of each.
  • I can walk a family member through the 10 modules we use every class and say why each one exists.
  • I can describe in one sentence what my end-of-year portfolio will contain and who sees it, and write one paragraph in my own voice that captures who I am as a historical thinker on Day 1.

TONIGHT'S WORK
  • Complete your F0 responses and submit them in Canvas.
  • Read Theme 1, page 18, in the eBook.

Topic F1: Geography Shapes Civilization

Event title

Assign to, one row per section

Preview
AP World History · Foundations
Topic F1: Geography Shapes Civilization
GGreen DayMonday, August 10 SSilver DayTuesday, August 11

OVERVIEW

Geography is the first layer of the AP World operating system. Before you can explain any state, empire, or trade network, you need the event that made all of them possible: the Neolithic Agricultural Revolution, the shift from hunting and gathering to farming. Today you build one causal chain — geography made farming possible, farming produced surplus, surplus produced civilization — and you learn to treat geography as an argument, not a backdrop.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain the Neolithic Agricultural Revolution, the shift from hunting and gathering to settled agriculture, and how geography made farming possible in certain river valleys and not in other environments.
  • I can explain how an agricultural surplus produced the characteristics of civilization: cities, specialized labor, government, writing, social classes, and organized religion.
  • I can write a short contextualization statement connecting a geographic condition to the rise of farming or civilization.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can describe how hunter-forager life differed from settled agricultural life, and name a specific geographic feature, a river, fertile soil, a domesticable species, that made the beginning of agriculture possible.
  • I can trace the causal chain from agricultural surplus to at least three characteristics of civilization.
  • I can write a contextualization sentence that identifies a geographic condition and explains how it shaped the shift to farming or the rise of a civilization.

TONIGHT'S WORK
  • Finish the Foundations 1 modules for Geography Shapes Civilization.
  • Read Theme 2, Cultural Developments and Interactions, pages 19 and 20, in the eBook.

Preview
AP World History · Foundations
Topic F2: Belief Systems & Cultural Exchange
GGreen DayWednesday, August 12 SSilver DayThursday, August 13

OVERVIEW

Confucianism, Daoism, Hinduism, Buddhism, Christianity, and Islam were never only private spiritual matters. They were public institutions that organized labor, legitimated authority, structured family life, funded education, and connected communities across enormous distances. Today you learn the core idea of each system, how each one spread, and how each one changed when it entered a new region. Seeing belief systems as institutions rather than only theologies is what lets you analyze them with real historical depth.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can identify the core beliefs and origins of the six major belief systems: Confucianism, Daoism, Hinduism, Buddhism, Christianity, and Islam.
  • I can explain how belief systems functioned as institutions that organized society, not just private faith.
  • I can trace how a belief system spread through trade networks, state adoption, or missionary activity, and compare how two of them adapted when they entered a new region (syncretism).

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can state the central idea of each of the six belief systems and where it originated.
  • I can identify a specific institutional function of a belief system, education, law, welfare, legitimacy, social order, and give a concrete historical example.
  • I can explain at least one mechanism by which a belief system spread, trade route, state adoption, missionary, civil service exam, or monastic network, and give a specific example of syncretism that shows how belief systems change as they travel.

TONIGHT'S WORK

Nothing tonight.

Topic F3: States, Power & Social Organization

Event title

Assign to, one row per section

Preview
AP World History · Foundations
Topic F3: States, Power & Social Organization
GGreen DayFriday, August 14 SSilver DayMonday, August 17

OVERVIEW

States are not natural. They are constructed solutions to specific problems: every state has to extract resources, defend territory, administer distant populations, and make its rule feel legitimate rather than merely forced. Persia, Han China, Greece, and Rome answered those same four problems in strikingly different ways, through tolerance and delegated satrapies, through centralized bureaucracy and the Mandate of Heaven, through citizen self-rule in the polis, and through law and expanding citizenship. If you can compare those four answers, you can analyze any state you meet in Units 1 through 9.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how Persia, Han China, Greece, and Rome each solved the core problems of extraction, defense, administration, and legitimacy, and name the specific tools of rule they used, satrapies, bureaucracy, the Mandate of Heaven, citizen democracy, Roman law and citizenship.
  • I can analyze how social hierarchies were constructed and who was excluded in at least two of these classical societies.
  • I can compare two classical states and explain a meaningful similarity or difference in how they organized power.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can name a specific tool of rule from one of the four classical civilizations, give an example, and explain the governance problem it solved.
  • I can explain one example of resistance or exclusion (the Yellow Turbans, Spartacus, Greek or Roman exclusion of non-citizens) and connect it to a limit of state power.
  • I can compare two of the four states by explaining how each answered the same problem differently, using a specific mechanism, not just "it helped the ruler" but how and why.

TONIGHT'S WORK

Nothing tonight.

Preview
AP World History · Foundations
Topic F4: Trade Networks & Innovation
GGreen DayTuesday, August 18 SSilver DayWednesday, August 19

OVERVIEW

Trade routes do not simply move goods. They are systems of human interaction that transform everything they touch. A Sogdian merchant carrying silk from Chang'an to Samarkand is also carrying Tang court aesthetics, Buddhist monastery patronage networks, diseases bred in crowded Chinese cities, and their own religious practice. The goods are the most visible layer, and the invisible layers are often the more consequential ones. Today you learn to see all of them at once.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how each of the four transregional routes operated, the Eurasian Silk Roads, the trans-Saharan caravan routes, the Indian Ocean sea lanes, and the Mediterranean sea lanes, including the climate and terrain each crossed, the goods it typically carried, and the communities who ran it.
  • I can name the technologies that made long-distance transport possible, a pack-animal technology such as the camel saddle, yoke, or stirrup and a maritime technology such as the lateen sail or the dhow, and I can identify specific non-goods that traveled the networks: crops and irrigation methods, disease pathogens, religious traditions, and people.
  • I can write a complexity argument explaining how trade networks caused multiple simultaneous changes across different regions.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can name all four required routes, give at least three specific port cities or oasis towns and explain each one's geographic function, and describe how the Indian Ocean monsoon worked, which months, which directions, which sailing routes.
  • I can name one pack-animal technology and one maritime technology with a date, and I can give at least two specific examples of non-goods traveling the networks, with dates and locations, including one religious tradition that was changed by the journey.
  • I can write a complexity paragraph that identifies multiple effects of a single trade network and explains how they connected across regions.

TONIGHT'S WORK

Nothing tonight.

Topic 1.1: Song China: Power, Prosperity, and the Scholar's World

Event title

Assign to, one row per section
SectionTaughtWork due

Silver DayThursday, August 27Monday, August 31
Preview
AP World History · Unit 1: The Global Tapestry
Topic 1.1: Song China: Power, Prosperity, and the Scholar's World
GGreen DayWednesday, August 26 SSilver DayThursday, August 27

OVERVIEW

Song China ran an empire through paperwork. Where other states of the period rewarded noble families or bought soldiers, the Song recruited officials through a written examination, sealed the candidates' names so the graders could not know whose paper they held, and rotated the winners between posts so that none of them could build a base. Today you follow that machinery, the Neo-Confucian revival that gave it a moral language, the commercial revolution that paid for it, and the northern frontier where the whole arrangement finally cracked. Hold onto the exam in particular: it is one half of a comparison Topic 1.2 will ask you to make.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how Song China used Confucianism, imperial bureaucracy, and civil service exams to maintain and justify rule.
  • I can describe how Chinese cultural traditions and Buddhism continued to shape East Asia and influence neighboring regions.
  • I can explain how agricultural innovation, infrastructure, and commercialization strengthened Song China's economy and connections to wider trade networks.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can use specific evidence such as bureaucracy, civil service exams, Confucianism, or Neo-Confucianism to explain how Song rulers organized power.
  • I can explain how Confucianism, Buddhism, and Chinese cultural traditions continued or changed as they shaped societies in East Asia.
  • I can connect Champa rice, the Grand Canal, paper money, trade, and production to population growth, urbanization, and commercial expansion.

TONIGHT'S WORK
  • Required eBook reading for Topic 1.2, Developments in Dar al-Islam (ebook/unit-1.html).
    • 01 The Unraveling of the Caliphate
    • 02 The Turkic Successor States
    • 03 How Islam Actually Spread
    • 04 The Knowledge Machine
    • 05 Who Was on Top, and Who Was Not recommended

Preview
AP World History · Unit 1: The Global Tapestry
Topic 1.2: Developments in Dar al-Islam
GGreen DayFriday, August 28 SSilver DayMonday, August 31

OVERVIEW

The Abbasid caliph did not fall in 1258. He had been powerless for three hundred years already, kept on his throne by the very soldiers who had taken his power, because the legitimacy attached to him was worth more to them intact than removed. Today you follow what grew in that gap: the Turkic states that formed inside a fragmenting caliphate, the merchants and Sufi teachers who carried Islam into regions no army ever reached, and the cheap paper, shared language, and endowed institutions that let scholarship survive the loss of its own capital. Dar al-Islam is this course's clearest case of cultural coherence outlasting political unity.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how systems of belief and their practices affected society in the period from c. 1200 to c. 1450.
  • I can explain the causes and effects of the rise of Islamic states over time.
  • I can explain the effects of intellectual innovation in Dar al-Islam.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can describe how Islamic states changed after Abbasid fragmentation and identify examples such as the Seljuk Empire, Mamluk Sultanate, and Delhi Sultanate.
  • I can explain how Islam spread through military expansion, merchants, missionaries, and Sufi networks.
  • I can connect scholarship, translation, paper-making, mathematics, medicine, astronomy, and geography to intellectual exchange.

TONIGHT'S WORK
  • Finish BeInTheRoom, the scholars council, if it did not fit in the block.
  • Required eBook reading for Topic 1.3, Developments in South and Southeast Asia (ebook/unit-1.html).
    • 01 South Asia After the Sultanate Arrived

AP World History · Unit 1: The Global Tapestry
Topic 1.3: Developments in South and Southeast Asia
GGreen DayTuesday, September 1 SSilver DayWednesday, September 2

OVERVIEW

South and Southeast Asia in this period is two problems side by side. Vijayanagara and the Delhi Sultanate were land states, built on rice, water control, and the revenue of farmed territory. Srivijaya, Majapahit, and Melaka were sea states, built on a strait, a monsoon, and the ability to tax whatever passed through. Today you learn what each kind of state needed in order to survive, and what Hinduism, Buddhism, and Islam each did for the rulers who adopted them. The comparison between the two kinds is the thing this topic is actually testing.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how Hinduism, Buddhism, and Islam shaped societies and states in South and Southeast Asia.
  • I can describe how states such as the Vijayanagara Empire, Delhi Sultanate, Srivijaya, Majapahit, and Khmer Empire used religion, trade, and administration to build power.
  • I can explain how Indian Ocean trade connected South and Southeast Asia to wider Afro-Eurasian networks.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can use specific evidence about Hinduism, Buddhism, Islam, temples, rulers, and merchants to explain how belief systems shaped society.
  • I can compare how land-based states (Vijayanagara, Khmer) and maritime states (Srivijaya, Majapahit) used religion and geography to build power.
  • I can connect trade routes, ports, monsoon winds, and merchant communities to political and cultural change in South and Southeast Asia.

TONIGHT'S WORK

Topic 1.4: State Building in the Americas
GGreen DayThursday, September 3 SSilver DayFriday, September 4

OVERVIEW

The Maya, the Mexica, and the Inca built three of the largest states of the period without a shared writing system between them, without the wheel in practical use, and, in the Inca case, without money. Today you follow how each one answered the same problems every state faces, extracting resources, holding distant territory, and making rule feel legitimate rather than merely forced: the Mexica through tribute, the Inca through labor owed to the state, the Maya through cities that competed rather than combined. The topic closes on the question the evidence forces, which is who wrote these societies down, and what that does to every claim you make about them.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how and why states in the Americas developed and changed over time.
  • I can describe how American state systems demonstrated continuity, innovation, diversity, and expanded in scope and reach.
  • I can identify evidence in a source that supports an argument about state building in the Americas.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can use evidence about Maya city-states, Mexica, Inca, Chaco, Mesa Verde, or Cahokia to explain state systems in the Americas.
  • I can explain continuity, innovation, diversity, or expansion in American state systems.
  • I can identify evidence used in a source to support an argument about American state building.

Topic 1.5: State Building in Africa

OVERVIEW

African states in this period were built on connection, not isolation. Mali and the Hausa city-states sat on the trans-Saharan routes, the Swahili coast on the Indian Ocean monsoon, Great Zimbabwe on gold moving toward that coast, and Ethiopia on a Christianity older than most of Europe's. Today you learn how each used trade, religion, and architecture to build authority, and you meet a case where the archaeology itself was pressured to produce a politically convenient answer about who built Great Zimbabwe. That last one is a lesson about evidence as much as about Africa.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how and why states in Africa developed and changed from c. 1200 to c. 1450.
  • I can describe how trade, religion, and geography shaped state power in Great Zimbabwe, Ethiopia, and the Hausa kingdoms.
  • I can explain how Islam and Christianity functioned as tools of governance, not just belief, in African states.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can use specific evidence about Great Zimbabwe's stone enclosures, gold trade, and Indian Ocean connections to explain how it built power.
  • I can explain how Ethiopia's Solomonic dynasty used Christianity and control of Red Sea trade to maintain independence and legitimacy.
  • I can describe how Hausa city-states used trans-Saharan trade and Islamic administration to build and exercise power.

Topic 1.6: Developments in Europe

OVERVIEW

Europe is this period's case of a region that did not centralize, and the useful question is what grew in the space where a large state did not. A Church with its own courts, its own revenue, and the power to excommunicate a king. Chartered towns that bought their independence. Guilds. Assemblies that traded money for a say in how it was spent. Today you follow all four, and then the plague, which did more to end serfdom than any monarch managed. Europe earns its place in this unit mostly as a contrast, so keep asking how each of these looks next to Song China or Dar al-Islam.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how European political structures developed in the period c. 1200 to c. 1450.
  • I can describe how Christianity, feudalism, manorialism, and cities shaped European society.
  • I can explain how Europe compared with other regions of Unit 1 in state power, belief systems, and economic organization.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can use evidence about monarchies, nobles, the Church, and decentralized power to explain European politics.
  • I can explain the roles of feudalism, manorialism, towns, guilds, and trade in European society.
  • I can compare Europe with Song China, Dar al-Islam, Africa, the Americas, or South and Southeast Asia.

Topic 2.1: The Silk Roads

Event title

SectionTaughtWork due

Preview
AP World History · Unit 2: Networks of Exchange
Topic 2.1: The Silk Roads
GGreen DayWednesday, September 16 SSilver DayThursday, September 17

OVERVIEW

Long-distance Silk Roads trade expanded after 1200 because rising demand for luxury goods made the journey worth financing while caravanserais, credit, banking houses, paper money, and periods of relative political stability reduced merchant risk and cost. Today you follow that economic chain from demand to easier exchange to the growth of trading cities such as Kashgar and Samarkand, then to producers in China, Persia, and India expanding output for distant markets.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain why Silk Roads trade expanded after 1200 by connecting demand, commercial practices, transportation infrastructure, and supporting political stability.
  • I can explain how caravanserai, credit, banking houses, and paper money reduced the risk and difficulty of long-distance trade.
  • I can explain how demand for luxury goods increased production and helped trading cities such as Kashgar and Samarkand grow.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can build a cause-and-effect chain: demand plus improved trade systems and lower political risk increased trade volume and geographic reach.

Indian Ocean exchange expanded because merchants learned to use predictable monsoon winds and improved maritime technologies such as the compass, astrolabe, and larger ship designs. Today you follow how that expanding system strengthened trading states and cities including the Swahili Coast, Gujarat, and Malacca, created diasporic merchant communities, and connected regions strongly enough for voyages such as Zheng He's to operate across an already mature network.

LEARNING TARGETS

  • I can explain how expanded Indian Ocean trade promoted powerful trading cities and states such as the Swahili Coast city-states, Gujarat, and the Sultanate of Malacca.
  • I can explain how diasporic merchant communities and Zheng He's voyages demonstrate the cultural and technological effects of intensified Indian Ocean exchange.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can explain how predictable monsoon winds and navigational or shipbuilding innovations lowered the risk and increased the range of maritime trade.

Expanded exchange networks changed culture as well as commerce. The same exchange networks that moved merchants and goods also moved living things.   • I can use bananas in Africa, new rice varieties in East Asia, and citrus in the Mediterranean as evidence of crop diffusion through exchange networks.

Europe borrowed tools from older worlds, the compass from China, the astrolabe and tables of the sky from Greek and Islamic astronomers, and the lateen sail from the Mediterranean, built new ships around them, and learned to ride the Atlantic's winds home. OVERVIEW

Last class, rulers paid for ships to cross the ocean. Today you find out what else those ships carried. Some things crossed on purpose, like horses, cattle, and wheat, some crossed by accident, like smallpox and the rats in the cargo, and some crossed with enslaved Africans carried by force. For each one, explain how it crossed and what it did to the people at the other end, in the Americas and in Africa, Asia, and Europe.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain what caused the Columbian Exchange: ships crossing the Atlantic, and later the Pacific, and coming back, carrying plants, animals, and germs, some on purpose and some by accident.
  • I can explain how diseases from the Eastern Hemisphere, such as smallpox, measles, and malaria, and disease vectors, such as rats and mosquitoes, crossed to the Americas, and why these diseases had catastrophic effects on many Indigenous populations.
  • I can explain the effects of the exchange on both hemispheres. In the Americas: animals and crops Europeans brought, foods enslaved Africans brought, and cash crops grown on plantations with coerced labor. In Afro-Eurasia: American staple crops that improved nutrition.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can state the cause of the Columbian Exchange and give one thing that crossed on purpose and one that crossed by accident.
  • I can name a disease and a disease vector, and give two reasons these diseases were so deadly in the Americas, including one about the conditions people lived in, such as war, forced labor, or hunger.
  • I can explain one effect in the Americas and one in Afro-Eurasia, each with a specific animal, crop, or food and the people it affected.

AP World History · Unit 4: Transoceanic Interconnections
Topic 4.4: Maritime Empires Established
GGreen DayThursday, November 5 SSilver DayFriday, November 6

OVERVIEW

Last class ended with a question: who would do the work in the new colonies, and who would rule? Today you find out, and the answer reaches Africa and Asia too. Rival European states built forts on the coasts and colonies in the Americas, but China and Japan set their own terms, Asian merchants kept trading, and Kongo and Asante grew stronger. For each case, explain what changed and what kept going, in who ruled, in work, and in slavery.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain why rival European states built maritime empires and trading posts, and how Kongo and Asante grew stronger through the new trade.
  • I can explain how Ming China and Tokugawa Japan limited European trade, and what changed and what continued in Indian Ocean trade after the Europeans arrived.
  • I can explain what continued and what changed in labor systems in the colonial Americas, from the Inca mit’a to encomienda, hacienda, indentured servitude, and chattel slavery.
  • I can explain how older forms of slavery continued in Africa while the plantation economy made slavery in the Americas far larger and different.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can name a political, religious, or economic rivalry behind the empires, and use a trading post or Kongo or Asante to explain one change in who held power.
  • I can explain one continuity in who set the terms of trade: how China or Japan kept control of trade with Europeans, or how a merchant group such as Gujaratis, Swahili Arabs, Omanis, or Javanese kept Indian Ocean trade going even after the Portuguese began forcing ships to buy the cartaz.
  • I can explain one labor system that continued in a new form and one that was new, and how each supplied workers for farms or mines.
  • I can explain one older form of slavery in Africa that continued and one way plantations changed slavery in the Americas, and why it changed.

Topic 4.5: Maritime Empires Maintained and Developed

Event title

Assign to, one row per section
SectionTaughtWork due

Silver DayTuesday, November 10Thursday, November 12
Preview
AP World History · Unit 4: Transoceanic Interconnections
Topic 4.5: Maritime Empires Maintained and Developed
GGreen DayMonday, November 9 SSilver DayTuesday, November 10

OVERVIEW

Last class, Europeans built empires from the sea. Today you find out how rulers made those empires pay. Follow the tools they built, mercantilist laws and companies that could go to war, then follow what those tools moved: silver pulled all the way to China, goods and enslaved people across the Atlantic, and more work for ordinary spinners and weavers. For each part, explain what was new and what kept going, then explain what the trade did to families in Africa and compare how religions spread, clashed and blended.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how European rulers used mercantilism and chartered joint-stock companies to make their empires pay and to compete with each other, and how economic disputes led to rivalries and wars.
  • I can explain what changed and what continued in networks of exchange from 1450 to 1750: silver pulled toward China, the Atlantic trading system, regional markets that kept flourishing, and peasant and artisan work that continued and grew.
  • I can explain how the trade in enslaved people changed families and communities in parts of Africa, and how Africans, Indigenous Americans, and Europeans all contributed to new mixed cultures in the Atlantic world.
  • I can compare how religions affected societies as contact grew: how existing religions spread, how contact caused religious conflict, and how new blended, or syncretic, beliefs and practices developed.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can explain how one mercantilist law or one joint-stock company, such as the VOC or the English East India Company, helped a ruler make an empire pay or compete with a rival, and name one rivalry that grew out of an economic dispute.
  • I can explain one change in networks of exchange (silver pulled toward China, or the Atlantic trading system) and one continuity (regional markets with their old merchants and ways, or peasant and artisan work that continued and grew).
  • I can explain one way the trade in enslaved people changed families in parts of Africa, and one example of cultural mixing in the Atlantic world that Africans, Indigenous Americans, and Europeans all contributed to.
  • I can use two examples to compare how religions spread, clashed, or blended, and say one way they were similar and one way they were different.

  • Finish Checkpoint 2, and any other required 4.5 module you did not complete in class.

Preview
AP World History · Unit 4: Transoceanic Interconnections
Topic 4.6: Internal and External Challenges to State Power
GGreen DayWednesday, November 11 SSilver DayThursday, November 12

OVERVIEW

Last class, rulers built tools to make their empires pay, and they reached further than ever. Today you find out who pushed back. Judges and nobles in France, peasants and Cossacks in Russia, a warrior kingdom in India, a queen in Africa, and Pueblo towns in New Mexico all resisted a state that was pushing on them, and enslaved people in Brazil, Jamaica and South Carolina organized to challenge the colonies that held them. For each case, explain what the state pushed for, who pushed back and how, and what happened next.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how states' push to expand and to centralize led different local groups to resist, using one case from Africa, Asia, or Europe and one from the Americas, and what that resistance changed.
  • I can explain how enslaved people in the Americas challenged the authorities over them through organized resistance, such as maroon communities and revolts, and how the authorities responded.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can explain, for one case from Africa, Asia, or Europe (the Fronde, Razin's revolt, the Marathas, or Njinga) and one from the Americas (the Pueblo Revolt or Metacom's War), what the state pushed for, which group pushed back and how, what happened next and what the resistance changed, and one way the two cases were alike.
  • I can explain how one maroon community (Palmares or the Jamaica Maroons) and one revolt (the Stono Rebellion) were organized, how the authorities responded to each, and one reason the responses differed.

Topic 4.7: Changing Social Hierarchies

Event title

Assign to, one row per section
SectionTaughtWork due
Green DayFriday, November 13Tuesday, November 17
Silver DayMonday, November 16Wednesday, November 18
Preview
AP World History · Unit 4: Transoceanic Interconnections
Topic 4.7: Changing Social Hierarchies
GGreen DayFriday, November 13 SSilver DayMonday, November 16

OVERVIEW

Last class, you saw people push back against growing states. Today you find out who ended up where. Every society still ranked people from top to bottom, but empires changed who stood on which rung: the Ottomans took in Jewish refugees that Spain pushed out, the Mughal emperor Akbar welcomed Hindu princes into his army, the Manchus conquered China and built a new elite, the casta system put Spanish-born officials at the top in the Americas, and stronger rulers squeezed old nobles in the Ottoman Empire, Russia, and France. For each case, explain what stayed the same and what changed.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain why some states welcomed or made use of different religious and ethnic groups, while others pushed groups out or limited them, using the Ottoman or Mughal Empire and one other case.
  • I can explain how conquest and new trade created new elites, such as the Manchu banners of Qing China and the Spanish-born and creole elites of the casta system in Spanish America.
  • I can explain how the power of old elites, such as Ottoman timar holders, Russian boyars, or European nobles, rose or fell as rulers grew stronger and centralized power, and what stayed the same.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can explain, for one state that made room for or made use of a group (the Ottoman Empire or Akbar's Mughal Empire) and one state that pushed out or limited a group (Spain or Qing China), what the state did and what it gained, and, for one of them, what changed for the group and what stayed the same.
  • I can explain how one of the new elites (the Qing banners, or the peninsulares and creoles at the top of the casta system) was made by conquest or new trade.
  • I can explain how the power of one old elite (Ottoman sipahis who held timars, Russian boyars, or French nobles) changed as rulers grew stronger, naming one thing it lost and one thing it kept, and one thing about the top of society that stayed the same.

TONIGHT'S WORK
  • Finish Checkpoint 2, and any other required 4.7 module you did not complete in class.

Topic 4.8: Continuity and Change from 1450 to 1750

OVERVIEW

Last class ended with a question: trade, work, and the social ladder all moved between 1450 and 1750, so which change mattered most, and what stayed the same? Today you answer it with an argument. Follow the new trade in sugar, silver, and cloth all the way to the people: the workers it needed, the society of masters and slaves it built on Barbados, and the villages it changed in Africa. LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how economic developments between 1450 and 1750, such as the new demand for sugar, silver, and cloth, increased the demand for workers, and how that demand was met.
  • I can explain how those economic developments changed social structures: who was forced to work, who rose to the top, and how families lived, in places such as Barbados, Spanish America, and West Central Africa.
  • I can write a thesis and a short argument about how much social structures changed between 1450 and 1750, and what stayed the same, connecting evidence from different Unit 4 topics.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can follow one economic development (plantation sugar, Potosí silver, or the demand for cloth) to the workers it needed.
  • I can explain one change that development made to a social structure, such as slavery for life in Barbados, the casta ranking, or villages in West Central Africa with more women than men.
  • I can write a thesis that names one change and one continuity, support it with evidence from at least three Unit 4 topics, and explain how two pieces of my evidence relate.

OVERVIEW

Covers Units 3 and 4 in full. Unit 3 is the land-based empires: how they expanded, how rulers ran their lands and justified their rule, and how belief systems changed and divided them. Topic 5.1: The Enlightenment

Event title

Assign to, one row per section
SectionTaughtWork due
Green DayMonday, November 30Wednesday, December 2
Silver DayTuesday, December 1Thursday, December 3
Preview
AP World History · Unit 5: Revolutions
Topic 5.1: The Enlightenment
GGreen DayMonday, November 30 SSilver DayTuesday, December 1

OVERVIEW

Last unit ended with a question: by 1750 the oceans were joined and states were stronger than ever, so who do those states belong to? Today you meet the writers who asked every king, church, and noble the same question: by what right? You will learn their new answers, natural rights, the social contract, and religious toleration, see how the ideas spread before the Atlantic revolutions, and follow them into the 1800s, as reformers ended slavery and serfdom, widened the vote, and women demanded equal rights. Then you decide how much had really changed by 1900.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain the new way of thinking Enlightenment writers used to question where rulers got their power, and at least one of their new ideas: natural rights, the social contract, or religious toleration.
  • I can explain how Enlightenment ideas spread and came before the revolutions in the Atlantic world, and how the idea that a state belongs to its people became loyalty to the nation.
  • I can explain how reform movements, pushed by Enlightenment ideas, religious faith, and other causes, ended slavery and serfdom, widened the vote, and demanded women's rights between 1750 and 1900, and what had still not changed by 1900.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can explain one new Enlightenment idea (natural rights, the social contract, or religious toleration), name a writer who argued it (Locke, Rousseau, or Voltaire), and explain how it challenged the old answer that rulers' power came from God, tradition, and birth.
  • I can explain one way Enlightenment ideas spread (books such as the Encyclopédie, salons, coffeehouses, or letters), explain what it means that the ideas came before the revolutions that began in 1775, 1789, 1791, and 1810, and explain how "the people" came to mean the nation.
  • I can choose one reform movement (abolition, the end of serfdom, the right to vote, or women's rights), explain what pushed it forward (Enlightenment ideas, religious faith, or another cause) with one piece of evidence (such as the 1787 antislavery society, Russia in 1861, Olympe de Gouges, Mary Wollstonecraft, or Seneca Falls), and name what it had changed by 1900 and one thing that had not.

TONIGHT'S WORK
  • Finish Checkpoint 2, and any other required 5.1 module you did not complete in class.

Topic 5.2: Nationalism and Revolutions

Event title

Assign to, one row per section
SectionTaughtWork due
Green DayWednesday, December 2Friday, December 4
Silver DayThursday, December 3Monday, December 7
Preview
AP World History · Unit 5: Revolutions
Topic 5.2: Nationalism and Revolutions
GGreen DayWednesday, December 2 SSilver DayThursday, December 3

OVERVIEW

By 1789 the new ideas about rights were everywhere educated people read, but ideas alone never overthrew a king. Today you find out what else it took: a grievance, the words to name it, and a chance to act, in America, France, Haiti, and Spanish America, and you see how each revolution helped another one start or win. Then you follow what they left behind, new countries, new ideas about government, and a new loyalty to the nation that joined Italy and Germany together and broke the Balkans away from the Ottoman Empire.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how a grievance, the words of a revolutionary document, and a chance to act came together to cause revolutions against kings and empires between 1750 and 1900.
  • I can explain what the American, French, Haitian, and Spanish American revolutions created, including independent states in the Americas and new ideas about government such as liberalism and democracy, and how each revolution helped another one start or win.
  • I can explain how a new loyalty to the nation, built on a shared language, religion, customs, and homeland, was used by governments and by nationalists to join some states together and to pull peoples away from empires.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can choose one revolution (American, French, Haitian, or Spanish American) and name its grievance (such as British taxes, noble privilege and bread prices, slavery, or creoles shut out of high office), its words (America: the Declaration of Independence; France: the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen; Haiti: that French declaration as free people of color claimed it, or Toussaint Louverture's proclamation of 1793; Spanish America: Bolívar's Letter from Jamaica, written five years into the fighting), and its chance (such as Britain's distance, a bankrupt king, a France in revolution, or Napoleon's invasion of Spain).
  • I can name what one revolution created (such as the United States, a republic under its 1787 Constitution, Haiti in 1804, or the independent countries of Spanish America by 1826), explain one link in the chain (such as France's debt from the American war, or Haiti's help to Bolívar in 1816), and explain liberalism or democracy as a new idea about government.
  • I can explain what a nation is (people who share a language, a religion, customs, and a homeland), give one example of a government using national loyalty (revolutionary France in 1793) or building a shared loyalty to hold back nationalism (Ottomanism), and give one example of nationalism joining states (Italy in 1861 or Germany in 1871) and one of it pulling a people away from an empire (Greece in 1830, or Serbia, Montenegro, or Romania in 1878).

TONIGHT'S WORK
  • Finish Checkpoint 2, and any other required 5.2 module you did not complete in class.

Topic 5.3: The Industrial Revolution Begins

Event title

Assign to, one row per section
SectionTaughtWork due
Green DayFriday, December 4Tuesday, December 8
Silver DayMonday, December 7Wednesday, December 9
Preview
AP World History · Unit 5: Revolutions
Topic 5.3: The Industrial Revolution Begins
GGreen DayFriday, December 4 SSilver DayMonday, December 7

OVERVIEW

Even before Paris argued about rights, a different revolution had begun in Britain: a change in how things were made. Today you find out why it began there. Nature gave Britain coal, iron, and water close together, and a shortage of wood that pushed it to coal. People built the rest: better farms, growing towns, laws that protected property, cotton from abroad, and money to invest. Then you see what the factory changed: it put the work in one place and gave each worker one small job.

LEARNING TARGETS
  • I can explain how Britain's environment (its coal, iron, and timber, and its rivers, coast, and canals) and the things people built (better farming, growing towns, laws that protected property, resources from abroad, and saved-up capital) worked together to cause industrial production to grow, starting in Britain.
  • I can explain how the factory system gathered production in a single place and split the work into specialized jobs, and why that let a mill make more goods.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  • I can explain two things nature gave Britain (such as coal and iron, the shortage of wood, or rivers, the coast, and canals) and two things people built (such as better farming, towns, patents, cotton from abroad, or saved-up money). For each one, I can say what it made cheaper or possible. I can show one way two of them worked together.
  • I can describe the putting-out system, explain how a mill like Arkwright's at Cromford (1771) brought workers to water-powered machines in one building, explain how the work in a cotton mill was split into steps (carding, drawing, roving, and spinning) with each worker tending one, use Adam Smith's pin workshop (1776) to explain why splitting the work made more goods, and connect the factory to one environmental factor, such as the water that turned its wheel.

TONIGHT'S WORK
  • Finish Checkpoint 2, and any other required 5.3 module you did not complete in class.
